text: London was a busy city with many timber buildings and narrow lanes. The Great Fire began in Thomas Farriner’s bakery in Pudding Lane, near the Thames, early on 2 September 1666. The precise way it caught fire is uncertain.

Samuel Pepys lived in London and wrote a diary. His account describes people taking belongings towards the river. A diary gives one person’s view. Objects can tell a different part of the story. We compare evidence instead of guessing.

People carried possessions into boats and carts. Others went to open fields. Local people also tried to fight the fire; London had no organised fire brigade like today. The fire was brought under control as the wind weakened and gaps between buildings helped slow it.

Many Londoners lost their homes. Rebuilding took years. New rules required outside walls of brick or stone. These materials already existed before the fire. Much of the city kept its old street layout; a whole new London did not appear overnight.
Become a street detective. Make a prediction, change one part of a paper street, then compare what happens. Your model explores one idea; it does not change the real story of 1666.
Where did the Great Fire begin? A bakery in Pudding Lane Inside the modern Big Ben tower In the middle of the river
Which helped the fire spread? The number of letters in London Dry conditions, strong wind and close buildings A modern electric railway
Why is Pepys’s diary useful? It contains every person’s thoughts It was written by someone who lived through the time It is a photograph of every street

A new picture shows dry wooden houses close together in a strong wind. What could help explain why a small fire spread? The dry timber, wind and nearby buildings worked together. Knowing the date explains how it moved between houses. Knowing who owned the first house explains how it spread.

You find a diary describing one family taking a chest to the river. Which claim can that entry support? Every family in London saved a chest. The writer described that family moving a possession. No one in London used a cart.

A picture shows a plan for brick outside walls after the fire. What should your museum label explain? This picture proves every new house was finished that day. It shows a rebuilding idea; putting new rules into practice took years. It proves brick was invented for the first time after the fire.
